before: Satan made the peoples' deeds attractive.
after: The focus joins a recurring account of earlier peoples misled by Satan before judgment.
reason: In 29:38, وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ leads to obstruction from the path; 16:63 repeats فَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ for nations before the Prophet. The same agent, recipients, and object make the focus part of a recurring historical formula.

before: Satan beautified their deeds and turned them aside.
after: The beautification becomes a false promise of protection that collapses at confrontation.
reason: The focus's وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ is repeated in 8:48, where Satan follows the adornment with لَا غَالِبَ لَكُمُ الْيَوْمَ and إِنِّي جَارٌ لَّكُمْ. The camps then see one another and he retreats, showing how the beautifying word works as seductive assurance.

before: They were people with insight even as they went astray.
after: The insight claim is placed against a community that became blind and deaf despite divine sight of its deeds.
reason: The focus closes with وَكَانُوا مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ, while 5:71 says people فَعَمُوا وَصَمُّوا after supposing no trial would come and then calls God بَصِيرٌ بِمَا يَعْمَلُونَ. Its sight-and-hearing language makes a sharp inverse: human perception fails while deeds remain fully seen.

before: They possessed insight while their deeds led them away.
after: Their failed human insight sits beneath God's encompassing sight of their actions.
reason: 29:38 calls the peoples مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ even as Satan deceives them; 57:4 ends by saying God is بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ. This is a real sight-and-deeds counterpoint, though the second verse speaks of divine observation rather than their human insight.

before: They were turned away from the recognized path.
after: The focus's path obstruction also appears as people bar others after trading away divine signs.
reason: The focus says فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ after Satan adorns their deeds; 9:9 has فَصَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِهِ after people sell God's signs for a small price. The repeated blocking verb and way noun make the focus's diversion legible as a public refusal of revelation too.

before: Satan's beautification ends by blocking them from the path.
after: The obstruction is shown operating through a socially respectable shield of false oaths.
reason: 29:38 makes being turned from the path the consequence of beautified deeds; 63:2 says people use أَيْمَانَهُمْ جُنَّةً and then فَصَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ. The oath-shield supplies a concrete social disguise for the same obstruction named in the focus.

before: Satan made their works attractive and the path was blocked.
after: The way's obstruction can also turn back on its agents by rendering their works astray.
reason: The focus links أَعْمَالَهُمْ with being diverted from السَّبِيلِ; 47:1 pairs those who وَصَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ with أَضَلَّ أَعْمَالَهُمْ. This adds the consequence that blocking the route leaves the blockers' own works lost.

before: They had insight but were turned from the path.
after: Knowing obstruction becomes a witnessed act: they bar believers while standing as witnesses themselves.
reason: The focus says the people were مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ yet were diverted; 3:99 asks why its addressees تَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ and adds وَأَنتُمْ شُهَدَاءُ. The witness language makes the path-blocking culpable despite available recognition, not a failure of access to evidence.

before: Satan's beautification led to obstruction from the path.
after: The same satanic obstruction is specified as loss of remembrance and prayer through intoxicants and gambling.
reason: The focus connects Satan's beautification to فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ; 5:91 states that Satan seeks to create hostility through wine and gambling and وَيَصُدَّكُمْ عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَعَنِ الصَّلَاةِ. The latter names concrete acts of worship from which the same adversary turns people away.

before: The definite Satan is the agent who turns them from the path.
after: The focus's named agent receives a direct warning as the one who must not be allowed to deter people.
reason: In the focus, ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ beautifies deeds and then turns the people away; 43:62 directly warns وَلَا يَصُدَّنَّكُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ and names him عَدُوٌّ مُّبِينٌ. The same agent-action pairing turns the focus's past account into a standing warning.

before: The evidence had become clear to them before the turn away.
after: Clear guidance followed by satanic persuasion explains how recognition can precede deliberate reversal.
reason: 47:25 says people turned back after مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الْهُدَى and then names ٱلشَّيْطَانُ سَوَّلَ لَهُمْ. That order closely activates the focus's clear evidence, Satan's role, and the paradox of people with insight nevertheless being diverted.

before: They were turned away from the path.
after: The focus's path can be heard against a concrete social road that Lot's people are said to cut.
reason: The focus uses فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ for diversion from the recognized way; 29:29 says تَقْطَعُونَ السَّبِيلَ. That wording gives the path image a concrete, social obstruction, although the two verses need not describe the same kind of blocking.

before: Their historical ruin followed despite insight and clear evidence.
after: The next generation in the list receives clear proofs and answers with arrogance, extending the focus's evidence-versus-response pattern.
reason: Immediately after the focus, 29:39 says Moses came to Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ, but they فَاسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ. The clear-proof word activates تَبَيَّنَ while the arrogant response shows that visible evidence does not ensure a receptive path.

before: Their ruined dwellings are visible evidence for the addressed audience.
after: The dwellings fit a wider Qur'anic image of signs located in the earth for the certain.
reason: 29:38 points to evidence مِن مَّسَاكِنِهِمْ; 51:20 says وَفِي الْأَرْضِ آيَاتٌ لِّلْمُوقِنِينَ. It supplies a broad terrestrial-sign frame, though it does not specify ruined buildings, so the link remains general.

before: Thamud is one of the named peoples whose dwellings testify after their ruin.
after: The repeated name places the focus's pair in a wider catalogue of past nations, without restating its misguidance mechanism.
reason: 25:38 explicitly lists وَعَادًا وَثَمُودَا, repeating the two proper names that open the focus. This confirms their place among the Qur'an's historical peoples but does not itself explain the focus's visible dwellings or satanic diversion.

before: Their deeds were beautified before they were turned from the way.
after: Lot's plea calls the opposing people corrupters, a broad moral label for the harmful deed-field in the focus.
reason: 29:30 calls Lot's opponents الْقَوْمَ الْمُفْسِدِينَ, while the focus shows a people whose أَعْمَالَهُمْ were beautified and led them from the path. The shared moral field is real but general; the prayer itself does not name the focus's mechanism.

before: The dwellings preserve evidence after the former inhabitants are gone.
after: The preceding Lot episode supplies another condemned settlement whose impending destruction belongs to the same warning sequence.
reason: In 29:31 the messengers announce إِنَّا مُهْلِكُو أَهْلِ هَذِهِ الْقَرْيَةِ because its people are unjust; the focus later points to the remains of other peoples' homes. This is a real but broad ruined-settlement parallel, not a direct account of the named dwellings.

before: Satan turned the people away from the path although they had insight.
after: The parallel exposes the self-deception: people are blocked from the way while believing themselves guided.
reason: The focus says فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ and closes وَكَانُوا مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ; 43:37 repeats لَيَصُدُّونَهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ and adds وَيَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ. The actual path and guidance words make the focus's insight paradox explicit as mistaken self-assurance.

before: Their dwellings make the evidence plain to those who see them.
after: The nearby Lot narrative says a clear sign was left from the city, giving the focus's surviving remains a local counterpart.
reason: 29:35 says God left مِنْهَا آيَةً بَيِّنَةً after the punishment of Lot's town; 29:38 says the truth became clear مِن مَّسَاكِنِهِمْ. The same-surah sequence joins surviving place-traces to a clear sign left for people able to reason.

before: Satan adorns deeds in a way that misleads their owners.
after: The shared adornment image gains a contrast: the heavens are beautified for observers, while deeds are beautified to misdirect.
reason: 37:6 uses زَيَّنَّا for the adornment of the lower heaven with stars; the focus uses وَزَيَّنَ for Satan's treatment of people's deeds. The same adornment image is clear, but the divine celestial object makes this a contrastive echo rather than a parallel cause of misguidance.

before: The former people's dwellings are the surviving evidence visible to others.
after: The focus's dwelling-witness is made concrete by the report that after Ad's destruction only their homes could be seen.
reason: 46:25 says the destructive wind left لَا يُرَى إِلَّا مَسَاكِنُهُمْ, using the same dwelling noun as the focus's مِن مَّسَاكِنِهِمْ. It gives a precise image of the people gone but their habitations remaining as visible testimony.

before: The destroyed peoples' dwellings remain as a sign for those who reflect.
after: The Lot passage likewise says a sign was left in the punished place for people who fear the consequence.
reason: The focus points to evidence from the former dwellings; 51:37 says وَتَرَكْنَا فِيهَا آيَةً for those who fear painful punishment after the Lot episode. The shared left-behind sign image ties the focus's material remains to a preserved warning.

before: Thamud's surviving dwellings show a trace after the people were destroyed.
after: The verse's claim that none of Thamud was spared sharpens the distinction between vanished people and the material trace in the focus.
reason: 53:51 names وَثَمُودَا and adds فَمَا أَبْقَىٰ, stressing that none of them remained; the focus nevertheless directs readers to مَسَاكِنِهِمْ. This is a pointed contrast between total human destruction and the surviving built trace, though the other verse does not mention those homes.

before: The former homes are evidence of what happened to their inhabitants.
after: A dwelling itself can function as a sign, as the Saba passage explicitly locates an ayah in its people's settlement.
reason: The focus says the truth became evident from their مَسَاكِنِهِمْ; 34:15 says لِسَبَإٍ فِي مَسْكَنِهِمْ آيَةٌ. The shared dwelling-and-sign pairing makes habitation itself a bearer of evidence, even though Saba's setting is not described as already ruined.

before: Satan turned the people away from the established path.
after: The path image gains a deliberate opposite: the human way is made easy before the focus describes it being obstructed.
reason: The focus's فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ gives the way as an obstruction target; 80:20 says ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ. The shared noun makes the focus's blockage stand against a path made accessible, a contrast of diversion with ease.

before: Satan beautifies deeds in a way that obscures sound judgment.
after: The same beauty-and-seeing frame contrasts a heaven adorned for observers with deeds adorned to mislead people who had insight.
reason: 15:16 says the constellations were adorned لِلنَّاظِرِينَ, while the focus says Satan وَزَيَّنَ the people's deeds despite their مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ state. The shared adornment and observer imagery creates a suggestive contrast between beauty that invites true looking and beauty that distorts moral appraisal.

before: Their deeds were beautified and they were diverted from the way.
after: The paired wording makes adornment's outcome explicit as blind wandering by people who reject the afterlife.
reason: 27:4 says زَيَّنَّا لَهُمْ أَعْمَالَهُمْ and then فَهُمْ يَعْمَهُونَ; the focus likewise connects Satan's adornment of أَعْمَالَهُمْ to being turned from السَّبِيلِ. The shared deed-and-beautification formula supplies wandering blindness as the cognitive result of the focus's diversion.

before: They could perceive, yet Satan still turned them from the path.
after: The path is paired with an inverse of insight: eyes can be physically blotted out so that seeing the way becomes impossible.
reason: The focus calls its people مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ while saying they were turned from السَّبِيلِ; 36:66 joins طَمَسْنَا عَلَى أَعْيُنِهِمْ to فَأَنَّى يُبْصِرُونَ as they race toward the path. The explicit eye, seeing, and route words make physical blindness a sharp counterpart to misused insight.

before: Their homes remain evidence after the people have gone.
after: The abandoned houses of other destroyed towns give the focus's visible dwellings a close material parallel.
reason: 28:58 says of destroyed villages فَتِلْكَ مَسَاكِنُهُمْ لَمْ تُسْكَن مِّن بَعْدِهِمْ, matching the focus's مِن مَّسَاكِنِهِمْ. Both make uninhabited houses the remaining trace after a community's judgment.

before: The remains of earlier generations' dwellings are public evidence.
after: Walking through the ruined houses is itself presented as guidance and signs for people of reason.
reason: 20:128 asks whether the people have been guided by generations God destroyed before them, whose dwellings they يَمْشُونَ فِي مَسَاكِنِهِمْ, and calls these آيَاتٍ لِأُولِي النُّهَى. This directly activates the focus's clear testimony from ruined habitations and its challenge to insight.

before: The destroyed peoples' homes stand as evidence of their failure.
after: The nearby spider parable shifts dwelling from visible remains to a fragile shelter that cannot secure its dependents.
reason: The focus's مَسَاكِنِهِمْ are material traces of past peoples; 29:41 describes the spider taking بَيْتًا and calls its house the weakest of homes. The shared dwelling image is real and locally adjacent, though the spider's reliance metaphor does not itself explain the ruined settlements.

before: The people were already described as possessing insight.
after: A future command to look makes the focus's claimed perception resonate with recognition that comes only later.
reason: The focus closes with مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ, while 37:175 commands وَأَبْصِرْهُمْ and promises فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ. The sight root creates a modest temporal contrast between apparent present insight and a future seeing that will be unavoidable.

before: Their insight did not keep them from being diverted.
after: After naming dwellings as signs, the verse asks whether people hear, shifting failed receptivity from sight to hearing.
reason: 32:26 says people walk among destroyed generations' dwellings and then asks أَفَلَا يَسْمَعُونَ; the focus instead calls its people مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ while they miss the path. This sensory shift is a weak but real reminder that exposure to evidence and claimed perception do not guarantee reception.

before: The evidence from the dwellings had become clear.
after: The shared clarity word echoes the focus's manifest evidence, though this verse names a clear Book rather than historical remains.
reason: The focus uses تَبَيَّنَ for evidence becoming clear; 43:2 calls the revelation الْكِتَابِ الْمُبِينِ. Their clarity language meets directly, but the distinct objects leave only a general echo between textual and material evidence.

before: Ad's people had insight and yet their course ended in ruin.
after: Their boast of strength and denial of signs show a concrete way a people can fail to see despite evidence.
reason: 41:15 names فَأَمَّا عَادٌ, says they arrogantly asked مَنْ أَشَدُّ مِنَّا قُوَّةً, and notes they denied God's signs. The focus's mention of Ad among the insightful but diverted makes this a specific example of confidence and apparent perception failing before evidence.

before: Their deeds were attractive to them before the path was obstructed.
after: The call to Midian not to act corruptly supplies a nearby moral warning before the focus's catalogue of failed peoples.
reason: 29:36 tells Midian not to تَعْثَوْا فِي الْأَرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ; the focus later portrays other communities whose أَعْمَالَهُمْ were beautified before diversion. The shared corruption field links the admonition to the ensuing warning, but does not identify the same people or cause.

before: Satan beautified their works before turning them from the way.
after: Another community's evil works are beautified and followed by withheld guidance, confirming the focus's moral pattern.
reason: The focus has وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ before obstruction; 9:37 says زُيِّنَ لَهُمْ سُوءُ أَعْمَالِهِمْ and closes وَاللَّهُ لَا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الْكَافِرِينَ. The repeated beautified-works formula directly joins the focus's deception to a loss of guidance.

before: Satan made the people's works and direction appear attractive.
after: Beautification is located inside the heart and attached to a false expectation, exposing its inward operation.
reason: The focus says Satan وَزَيَّنَ their deeds; 48:12 says وَزُيِّنَ ذَٰلِكَ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ before describing a bad assumption and a people ruined. The inner-heart wording makes the focus's adornment more than outward appearance: it can reshape the judgment from within.

before: They were turned away from the recognized route.
after: Pilgrims approach from every distant pass, a weak counter-image of paths opened toward worship rather than obstructed.
reason: 22:27 pictures people arriving for pilgrimage مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ, while the focus says Satan turned people from السَّبِيلِ. The travel-route image meets the focus's path, but this verse does not use the same noun or describe misdirection, so the contrast remains modest.

before: Satan adorns deeds in a way that misleads their owners.
after: Earthly adornment is recast as a divine test of deeds, contrasting the test's purpose with Satan's corrupting beautification.
reason: The focus says Satan وَزَيَّنَ people's أَعْمَالَهُمْ and thereby obstructed them; 18:7 calls what is on earth زِينَةً لَّهَا and states that it tests أَيُّهُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا. The shared adornment-and-deeds image distinguishes a created test from satanic beautification that distorts judgment.
